EOP-10.renderedBody:
Amendment to this story's scope, from the corrected game rules.

The product requirements document was corrected after the real Elevation of Privilege rules were established from primary sources. One consequence lands here.

Assign a stable seat order when a player joins. Elevation of Privilege is a trick-taking game. Play proceeds clockwise, and the winner of each trick leads the next one. That means "who plays next" is derived by walking round the table from the current player, so the table itself must be an ordered structure. A Player therefore needs a seatOrder integer, assigned at the moment of joining and stable for the life of the session. This is load-bearing domain data, not bookkeeping - without it the turn sequence in EOP-14 cannot be computed at all.

Two constraints follow. Seat order must not be re-derived from a database sort or from join timestamps at read time, because a disconnect and reconnect must not move a player around the table. And it must survive the session being reloaded from PostgreSQL, since resuming mid-trick is a hard requirement.

Dealing the deck is not in this story. It belongs to EOP-14, which covers dealing the whole deck evenly into per-player hands at game start. Note there is no draw pile in this game - the deck is exhausted by the deal - so nothing in this story should model a remaining-deck or draw-pile concept.

Section 5 of docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md carries the corrected domain model and is the source of truth over this ticket.

EOP-10.renderedBody:
Session lifecycle is complete and open for review as PR #35. Behind eop.features.session-lifecycle, which stays off in the deployed stack — merging this releases nothing.

Edited to repair formatting. Jira reads a bare ADR-NNN token as an issue key and links it to an issue that does not exist, which also broke the emphasis around each one. Monospace suppresses it, so the ADR references below are in backticks — worth knowing for the next comment that cites one.

Decisions this ticket turned from accepted into implemented (ADR index updated with the evidence for each):

  • ADR-013 — feature flags via configuration properties. The flag withholds the controller bean through @ConditionalOnProperty rather than branching inside a request. A test asserts the bean is absent and all five routes 404, so the mechanism is pinned and not just the symptom.
  • ADR-014 — real-time transport via SSE. One endpoint publishes state; the stream announces that something changed and never what. A reconnecting client therefore takes the same path it took on first load, and there is exactly one producer of state to keep correct.
  • ADR-015 — server-issued opaque token. Issued once on admission, 43 characters, stored only as a SHA-256 digest. Sent in a header, never in a URL, because a query parameter would land in every proxy log. IdentityTokenHash.toString() is a constant so a careless log line cannot print one, and no response shape has a field for the digest.
  • ADR-018 — UUID v7 through an application port. Identifiers are minted in the use case, not at flush, so the aggregate knows its own identity before it is stored. A test pins the version nibble, the variant bits and time ordering across 2,000 draws, so a Hibernate upgrade that quietly reverted to version 4 fails the build.
  • ADR-019 — session lifecycle, join codes, header-only stream auth. Crockford base32, seat contention settled by a unique index rather than a lock.

The entropy and throttling tradeoff, recorded because it constrains anything built on top. A six-character Crockford base32 code is about thirty bits. That is short enough to read aloud over a video call, which is the whole point of it, and short enough to enumerate if the endpoint answers honestly. So it does not: a malformed code, a well-formed code nobody holds, and a code belonging to a session that has moved on all produce one indistinguishable refusal, identical in status, title and detail. JoinCode.parse returns an empty optional rather than throwing precisely so that "that is not a code" cannot be told apart from "no session has that code".

Guessing is then throttled per client address and per normalised code — ten and thirty failures a minute. Two consequences worth stating plainly:

  • Only failures are counted. A popular lobby cannot throttle its own players, and a successful join is never charged. The limiter is a guess-rate limit, not a request-rate limit.
  • The limiter is in-memory, so it is per instance. Correct at one instance, which is what ADR-012 deploys. It is the first thing to revisit if a second instance ever appears, because the effective allowance multiplies by the instance count. Recorded here rather than left as a surprise.

Normalisation feeds the throttle too: the code bucket is the parsed code, so abc230, ABC23O and " abc23o " share one counter and an attacker gains nothing by varying spelling.

Two defects the tests exposed, both fixed on this branch.

  1. The seventh player got 400 "Invalid request" leaking an internal invariant instead of 409 "Session is full" — nextSeatOrder() returned the player count regardless of capacity, so the seat-range guard fired before the capacity check, and the handler for SessionFullException was mapping an exception the API could not actually emit. Fixed in the domain: a full table has no next seat.
  2. SessionStateDto shared the caller's mutable player list. SpotBugs failed the build on it; the constructor now copies. It surfaced only at close-out because the feature commits were checked with test rather than verify — worth remembering as a habit, not just a fact.

A production Javadoc claim was also corrected rather than believed: handleUnknownJoinCode said every failed lookup returns a byte-identical response, and it does not, because Spring populates instance with the request URI. The security property is intact — instance echoes only the caller's own input — and the test now pins what is load-bearing instead of what was merely written down.

Verification. ./mvnw verify green: 298 tests, 0 failures, instruction coverage 97.34% against the 0.80 floor, checkstyle/spotbugs/enforcer clean.

Also run against the real stack — PostgreSQL 17 behind Caddy — because a green suite on H2 is not the same claim. Migration 003 applied cleanly to PostgreSQL with ddl-auto: validate accepting the mappings, so the schema is now proven on both engines. A live curl -N stream through the proxy carried retry:3000, :subscribed, repeated :heartbeat comments, two player-joined events and a game-started. It survives a browser's Accept-Encoding: gzip as well, since Caddy excludes text/event-stream from compression — worth knowing, because a proxy that buffered it would break the feature without breaking a single test.

Not done here, deliberately. No front end consumes these endpoints yet, so the flag flip belongs to the lobby UI ticket — the one that can actually verify it end to end. ADR-012 stays Partly implemented; Terraform has still never been applied.

EOP-14.renderedBody:
Tech Lead — delivery plan and three decisions confirmed before implementation.

Correction to this ticket's text. The description closes with "Also needs the concurrency-control decision, number 017." That reference is wrong: ADR-017 is Frontend Delivery Topology. The concurrency-control decision is [ADR-020](docs/adr/ADR-020-session-concurrency-control.md) — Concurrency Control by Compare-and-Set on `status`, Not by Optimistic Locking. This matters more than a typo, because ADR-020 exists specifically to warn that the @Version column on GameSessionJpaEntity is bookkeeping and not the enforcement mechanism. Implementation of this story must use status-guarded conditional UPDATE with rows-affected checks plus unique constraints — not JPA optimistic locking.

Decision 1 — the deal remainder. 78 cards divides evenly for 3 players (26 each) and 6 players (13 each), but leaves a remainder for 4 players (19 each, remainder 2) and 5 players (15 each, remainder 3). Neither the PRD nor this ticket specified the rule.

Resolved: every card is dealt; the extras go to seats in ascending order. The alternative — setting the remainder aside undealt — carries a latent defect: the lowest-ranked Tampering card can land in the discard, at which point "the holder of the lowest-ranked Tampering card leads the first trick" has no holder, and the opening lead silently requires a fallback branch. Dealing every card makes the opening-lead rule always resolve, matches how the physical deck is dealt, and keeps maximum threat coverage in play, which is the purpose of the deck.

Accepted consequence: hands are unequal, so the final trick is short. This is already sanctioned by PRD §3.3, whose end condition is players running out of "time, cards, or ways to connect their threats to the system." The domain will therefore define a trick as one card from each player who still holds cards, not as a fixed card count.

Decision 2 — where the current leader lives. PRD §5 lists a GameState block (currentLeader, currentTrick) with no corresponding entity, and GameSession is an immutable aggregate root. Resolved: the current leader's seat is stored on `game_session`. It gives the turn-order guard a single row to compare-and-set against, which is what makes the concurrency requirement in this ticket provable rather than asserted; and the opening leader has to be persisted somewhere regardless.

Decision 3 — this XL story ships as five PRs, not one. A single XL pull request breaks trunk-based development. Five short-lived branches off main, each merged and deployed on its own, all behind a new eop.features.trick-play flag defaulting to false (ADR-013):

Slice Content
A Pure domain: Hand, Trick, TrickPlay, follow-suit legality, trump resolution, derived opening lead. No framework imports, no schema.
B Liquibase changeset 004 for hand/trick/trick_play before the JPA entities, plus ports and adapters. Additive, no behaviour change.
C Dealing wired into session start behind the flag; endpoint returning the caller's own hand.
D OpenAPI document updated before any controller code; play-a-card endpoint; follow-suit and out-of-turn rejected server-side against the identity credential; RFC 9457 errors; the genuinely concurrent double-play test.
E Trick resolution wired, winner leads next trick, SSE events, flag default flipped under review.

Every slice takes all five Definition-of-Done gate approvals. Scoring remains out of scope — that is EOP-15.

The opening lead will be derived at runtime from the cards actually dealt. A literal 2 or 3 anywhere in the implementation is a defect, per this ticket and PRD §3.3.

Decisions 1 and 2 are being recorded as ADR-023. Slice A is in progress on branch EOP-14-trick-domain.

Second defect in this ticket's description, found during Slice A review.

The description still says the deck "is dealt evenly between players". That contradicts the very next requirement in the same paragraph, which says any remainder must be handled explicitly — if the deal were even there would be no remainder to handle. 78 cards divide evenly only at three players (26 each) and six (13 each); at four it is 20/20/19/19 and at five 16/16/16/15/15.

The confirmed decision, recorded in ADR-023 and now implemented, is that the whole deck is dealt out with the remainder going to the lowest seat numbers. "Whole deck" is the load-bearing half of the source sentence — it is what makes "there is no shared draw pile" true — and "evenly" is the incidental descriptor that cannot hold at four or five players. PRD §3.3 has been amended accordingly; this ticket has not, so anyone reading only the ticket would conclude the implementation is wrong.

Consequences already accepted: hands are unequal, the final trick is short, and a trick is therefore one card from each seat that still holds cards rather than a fixed count.

Together with the ADR-017 → ADR-020 correction in my earlier comment, that is two stale statements in this description. Both are recorded here rather than silently edited.

EOP-14.renderedBody:
Third stale statement in this description — recorded, not edited.

The description says, in the trump paragraph, that "The winner leads the next trick." That is the third statement in this ticket that the implemented rules contradict, and it is the one this story's central remediation was about.

It is only true while every seat still holds a card. Because every card is dealt and the remainder goes to the lowest seats (ADR-023, decision 1), hands are unequal at four and five players — at four players seats 0 and 1 hold twenty cards and seats 2 and 3 hold nineteen. So a seat can play its last card and win the trick it played it into. After trick nineteen, a win by seat 2 or 3 leaves the winner holding nothing while two seats each still hold one card.

Handing the lead back to that winner opens a trick nobody can ever play into: no seat can legally play, the trick is not complete because it has no plays, and the game stops with no exception, no error and nothing to log. That is not a hypothetical — it is a certain configuration at four and five players whenever a short-handed seat takes the penultimate trick.

The implemented rule is: the lead passes to the winner if the winner still holds a card, and otherwise to the next seat clockwise from the winner that does. Trick.nextLeaderSeat(seatsHoldingCards) answers it, and returns empty when no seat holds a card — one of the three end conditions in PRD §3.3. The method that answers "who took this trick" is deliberately called winningSeat() rather than nextLeaderSeat(), so that reaching for the winner is no longer the path of least resistance.

This was caught by @architecture-guardian reviewing its own ADR against the code, one section away from where the ADR had named the same class of defect.

Both the ADR and PRD §3.3 now carry dated deviation notes. Slice E, which wires lead passing, must implement the rule above rather than the sentence in this description.

For the record, the three corrections now tracked against this description are:

  • ADR-017 → ADR-020 for the concurrency-control decision (comment 10204). ADR-017 is Frontend Delivery Topology.
  • "dealt evenly between players" contradicting the same paragraph's own requirement that a remainder be handled explicitly (comment 10237).
  • "The winner leads the next trick" — this comment.

The description is left as written; the code, ADR-023 and PRD §3.3 are the authorities.

EOP-14.renderedBody:
Slice C1 complete — EOP-14 remains In Progress

PR #46 is open for Slice C1 (persistence), all five DoD gates approved on 7c7208e. This does not close EOP-14. Three of the five slices remain: C2 (use cases), D (endpoints + OpenAPI), E (resolution, SSE, flag flip).

What Slice C1 ships

Ports HandRepository/TrickRepository, TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter implementing both, JPA mappings for all five trick-play tables, changeset 005 range bounds, eight domain exception types with RFC 9457 mappings, and three compare-and-set session updates. 27 commits, 45 files, +6555/-66.

./mvnw verify — 722 tests, 0 failures, exit 0. Checkstyle 0, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo gate met.

Containment has changed and this matters for planning. All five tables are now mapped and reachable by any bean that injects either port. The old containment — "no entity, adapter or route" — is false as of this slice. What remains is no use case and no route, which is why eop.features.trick-play becomes a genuine merge precondition for C2 rather than a formality.

Two defects review found that the build did not

  1. A replayed trick resolution answered 500. Reachable on an ordinary hand, not an exotic one: advanceLeaderSeat sets current_leader_seat where it already equals the seat it compared against, so whenever the seat that led a trick also wins it the guard is idempotent and a replay passes it. The winner update's winner_play_id IS NULL predicate is what actually refuses. Now 409. This means trick resolution serialises on the `trick` row, not the session row — the one place in the design where the contended row is not game_session. Recorded in ADR-020.
  1. The port `@throws` contracts were wrong in both directions — declaring an exception a path cannot raise, and omitting two the test suite proved it does. All three write methods now declare everything their shared zero-rows helper can return.

New decision record

ADR-024 — one adapter implements both ports, and neither port authorises anybody. No method takes an acting player, so none can. The seat check is a check on the row, not the requester. This is the correction of an earlier comment that claimed otherwise.

Slice C2 obligations, carried explicitly

These are the ones where nothing in C1 fails if C2 forgets them:

  • Authorise the requester in every use case, deriving the acting player from the authenticated identity and refusing a caller-supplied seat. assertSeated looks exactly like an authorisation gate and is not one.
  • Cross-session scoping on the play, deal and delete paths, for cards as well as seats — the composite keys prove a player holds that seat somewhere, not at this table.
  • `trick.leader_seat` has no CHECK constraint — refused only by the domain on read. The other three seat columns got theirs in changeset 005.
  • `fk_trick_winner_play ON DELETE SET NULL` silently unresolves a trick if a winning play is deleted directly; only a comment prevents it today.
  • `eop.features.trick-play` in front of the new route, defaulted false.
  • `mentions` matches a constraint name by substring, not equality — a future name containing an existing one would be answered as the existing domain exception instead of failing loudly.

Description corrections

The three stale statements flagged earlier still stand as corrections and are now implemented as described: the concurrency decision is ADR-020, not 017; the whole deck is dealt with the remainder to the lowest seats, so hands are unequal and a trick is one card from each seat still holding cards; and the lead passes to the winner only if the winner still holds a card, otherwise to the next seat clockwise that does.

Next: merge #46, then Slice C2.

EOP-14.renderedBody:
Slice C2 (use cases) — ready for review: PR #47

Fourth of five. Branch EOP-14-slice-c2-use-cases, seven commits, HEAD 86f77db. EOP-14 stays In Progress — Slices D and E are still to come.

Shipped

DealHandsUseCase (facilitator only, returns void), PlayCardUseCase (+ PlayCardCommand), ResolveTrickUseCase (any seated member), the DeckShuffler port with SecureRandomDeckShuffler, CardRepository.findWholeDeck(), NoTrickToResolveException and TrickNotCompleteException with 409 mappings, and eop.features.trick-play (default false) gating all three beans. No HTTP route — that is the slice boundary, and it is Slice D's.

./mvnw verify: 774 tests, 0 failures, Checkstyle 0, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo met.

C1's four obligations are discharged

  1. Authorise the requester first, in every use case — done, and each has a test asserting a stranger is refused before any hand is read, asserted on the repository double's read log. This is the ADR-024 obligation that no port could enforce and no C1 test failed for.
  2. Cross-session scoping — closed by construction rather than validation: one sessionId scopes every read and write, and the trickId handed to appendPlay can only come from a session-scoped read.
  3. `eop.features.trick-play` — added, default false, gating the beans rather than a route, with tests in both positions.
  4. trick.leader_seat still has no CHECK constraint. Reassigned off C2 in ADR-023 with the reason recorded: C2 ships no changeset, and adding one here would put a migration in a PR whose claim is that it changes no schema.

One correction to the record, worth reading

ADR-025's original central claim was false and is retracted. It had argued the seam between starting a session and dealing was forced, because the two writes could not share a transaction without putting org.springframework.transaction into the use-case layer. An architecture review refuted it: a @Transactional composer in the outer ring joins two already-transactional adapter methods through REQUIRED propagation with no import inside usecase. The seam is chosen, not forced. The real reason for two calls is that StartSessionUseCase publishes GAME_STARTED over in-process SSE, and no transaction rolls back a delivered frame — so a composed transaction would trade a recoverable inconsistency (started but undealt, and idempotently retryable) for an unrecoverable one (every subscriber told a game started that was never dealt).

That claim was then hunted across the whole repository and found in eight places, including production javadoc in TrickRepository and TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter. All are now retracted in place rather than deleted, because a changelog and an ADR are records of what was believed at the time.

Definition of Done — five of five, all verdicts on the final commit

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE — rejected once, two MAJOR coverage gaps closed
@tester-api APPROVE — one NIT closed
@security-auditor APPROVE — one MEDIUM closed
@code-reviewer APPROVE — three suggestions applied
@architecture-guardian APPROVE — rejected three times; twelve, five and four findings closed

The security MEDIUM is worth naming: openTrick committed a trick row before TrickPlay's constructor measured the caller's text, so an over-long note or a 21-component list left a committed orphan trick and then threw. The candidate is now built before any write, pinned by a test.

Handoff — nothing in the repository fails if these are forgotten

Slice D owes:

  • Hand-author the three routes in docs/api/openapi.yml before the controllers (contract-first, ADR-004).
  • Gate the route on eop.features.trick-play, the same flag.
  • Mint the SessionEventType constants. C2 deliberately adds none: those constants carry the name in the event: field of an SSE frame, the name is fixed by openapi.yml, and minting one in a slice that publishes no contract only guarantees a rename. Until then a client learns of a deal, a play or a resolution only by re-reading — the stream is silent for a whole trick.
  • Flip nothing: the flag stays false on merge.

Slice E owes:

  • End-of-hand detection. ResolveTrickUseCase writes the winning seat as the next leader when no seat holds a card, because the port takes an int and rejects anything outside seat range. Harmless while no seat can play, and both branches are pinned by tests. Find that line by its expression — resolved.nextLeaderSeat(seatsHoldingCards).orElse(resolved.winningSeat()) — not by its line number: the documents previously pinned a line number that had drifted onto an integrity guard, and following it literally would have deleted the guard.
  • Pass a SessionEventPublisher in and wire the broadcast.

Known limitations, each explicitly accepted by a reviewer

  • No use-case logging anywhere — all ten use cases, not just the three new ones, while .opencode/rules/observability.md requires INFO at operation boundaries and audit logging for game-affecting actions. New ADR-026 (Proposed) holds the obligation, names all ten classes, and weighs four arrangements, because the obvious fix — SLF4J inside usecase — would breach clean-architecture.md. This wants its own story.
  • PlayCardUseCase.execute is 67 lines against ~31 for its siblings.
  • No ArchUnit or package-dependency test enforces the inward dependency rule, and checkstyle.xml declares no complexity module — both are reviewer-enforced only.
  • The orphan-trick window is closed by an argument, not a mechanism. The durable fix persists a trick and its first play in one call, which changes the TrickRepository contract.

Process note

.opencode/rules/ holds fifteen rule files. Only feature-flags.md and versioning.md were pointed at for this slice, so nine were never read at the start — observability.md among them, which is why two gates had to raise a binding rule I had initially dismissed. Worth fixing in the agent brief rather than rediscovering per slice.

GET /hand and a new ReadOwnHandUseCase (the eleventh use case) were added because Slice C promised "an endpoint returning the caller's own hand" and neither C1 nor C2 shipped it — without it a dealt player cannot see their cards, so the flag could never be flipped. It needed no new port method; the port count is unchanged at ten.

The path is singular on purpose, departing from the plural-noun rule, and that is now recorded in ADR-027: /hands would advertise a collection of every hand, which is the one operation that must never exist. The ADR forbids it rather than merely declining to use it.

⚠️ Hard handoff to Slice E — read this before planning it

1. The flag cannot be flipped by Slice E's stated scope alone. TrickDto deliberately publishes no whose turn it is, no is the trick complete, no which seat leads next. All three need seatsHoldingCards from Hands, which the use cases do not return and which a controller must not fetch from a second aggregate. With only one's own hand and the trick returned from one's own play, no client can learn whose turn it is.

Slice E must add {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

/tricks/current}} exposing seatToPlay, complete and nextLeaderSeat, or the feature flag can never be turned on.

2. ADR-026 is now a predecessor of the flag-on story, not a parallel backlog item. @security-auditor made this a condition of approval: dealing, playing and resolving are the product's first competitively meaningful writes, they are now reachable over HTTP, and they are entirely unaudited. A dispute over who played what would have nothing to appeal to. Recorded in ADR-026's Consequences.

3. Find `ResolveTrickUseCase`'s placeholder by its expression, never by line number: resolved.nextLeaderSeat(seatsHoldingCards).orElse(resolved.winningSeat()).

4. Three SSE names are minted but not emitted — hand-dealt, card-played, trick-resolved — as SessionEventType constants and members of the contract's SessionEvent.type enum, marked reserved. Wiring SessionEventPublisher is Slice E's. Until then the stream is silent for a whole trick. A test reads the contract as text so the enum and the contract cannot drift.

Two production defects found by writing the tests

  1. PlayCardRequest.threatLinked is now a boxed Boolean normalised to false. An absent primitive record component makes the deserialiser answer 400, so a field the contract published as optional was mandatory in practice — the server breaking its own published contract.
  2. The compact constructor copies components with List.copyOf, which refuses a null entry at the boundary. @Size waves a null element through.

Tests

850 in the build, 0 failures. Eighty-six touched by this slice, sixty-four new. The headline obligation — the genuinely concurrent double-play through the real HTTP layer — passes: two threads, one seat, two different cards, exactly one 201 and one 409, and the loser's card back in its hand.

That refusal assertion was wrong three times by trying to name the rule. There are at least three correct refusals depending on where the loser is when the winner commits: the trick's sequence constraint while opening it, the seat constraint while appending to it, and the domain's own turn check when the loser re-reads an opened trick. Slice E complete — all five DoD gates approved, PR #49 open

Branch EOP-14-slice-e · commits b39e6a7 (OpenAPI contract, alone and first) then 43f0cbc ( EOP-14 Done feat: report the state of play and the end of a hand) · PR https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/49 · 34 files changed, 1564 insertions, 257 deletions.

./mvnw clean verify → 893 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped; SpotBugs BugInstance size is 0; JaCoCo all coverage checks met over 109 classes.

What Slice E delivers

  1. *`GET /api/v1/sessions/ {sessionId}/tricks/current`* — new GetTrickStateUseCase + TrickState + TrickStateDto, publishing seatToPlay, complete, nextLeaderSeat and handComplete. This was the obligation inherited from Slice D: TrickDto deliberately answers none of the three, so before this route no client could learn whose turn it was and the flag could never have been turned on. seatToPlay and nextLeaderSeat come from different authorities (the cards in the trick vs the seat the session row records as leading) and are deliberately not reconciled, because a disagreement is a defect a client is entitled to notice.
    # End of hand recognised. TrickRepository.recordResolution's next-leader parameter widened int → OptionalInt; the Slice D placeholder .orElse(resolved.winningSeat()) is gone; a played-out hand records current_leader_seat = NULL. No new changeset — changeset 005's CHECK already permits NULL.
    # `HandCompleteException` → 409 "Hand complete", guarded in PlayCardUseCase by Hands.allEmpty() (its first caller), so a play into a spent hand is refused by name rather than by the misleading 422 an empty hand would otherwise produce. sessionMoved gained a sixth answer telling a played-out hand from an undealt one; no production caller reaches it, and it exists because the branch otherwise answers a lie.
    # The three declared-but-unpublished SSE names are now emitted — hand-dealt, card-played, trick-resolved — each after its write returns, so a refused operation announces nothing.

    h3. Scope decisions, recorded in ADR-028 (new, Accepted)

    * `eop.features.trick-play` stays `false`. Turning it on is its own story, whose predecessors are ADR-026 (use-case observability, still Proposed), EOP-48 (SessionController's missing havingValue) and EOP-15 (scoring). Merging behind a false flag exposes nothing: both flag positions now assert the same six beans and five routes.
    * EOP-14 does not move the session to `COMPLETED`. That word is documented as "every trick played and the score is final", and this story computes no score, so EOP-15 owns that transition. Consequence stated honestly: a client watching only {{GET /api/v1/sessions/{sessionId}

    }} never sees a session finish.

Gate verdicts

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE — 6 MINOR, 4 closed
@tester-api APPROVE — caught the contract claiming eleven 409 titles against thirteen handlers
@security-auditor APPROVE — no BLOCKER/MAJOR; seven conditions recorded for flag-on, not merge
@code-reviewer APPROVE — zero framework imports in entity/usecase confirmed
@architecture-guardian APPROVE on its fourth review, after three rejections

Gate 5 rejected three times, each time for documentation asserting in the present tense that this slice's work was outstanding. docs/architecture/C4-Diagrams.md and runtime-view.md had never been touched and described a system that did not exist — including a sequence-diagram note quoting deleted source as current. ADRs 013, 020, 023, 025, 026 and 027 were amended in place with dated notes. The last surviving instance was found only by searching "flipped" where earlier passes had searched "turned on".

Disclosed honestly

  • One unexplained red run inside TrickControllerIntegrationTest.PlayingACard. Its log and surefire report were lost before being read, so the failing method is permanently unknown; it never reproduced in 16+ runs. A genuine latent shuffle-dependence in shouldRefuseAPlayThatDoesNotFollowSuit was found and fixed, but not proven to have been the cause.
  • A merge-versus-insert subtlety found by writing a test: the deal-once gate rests on uq_hand_session_seat and on a deal minting fresh hand identifiers — reusing them makes the write a merge, and the first version of that test watched a second deal silently succeed.
  • Open by choice: HandCompleteException(null) would render a null in its message; DealHandsUseCaseTest:197 uses containsSubsequence where ordering is already pinned elsewhere; the state route's integration tests read with the facilitator's token.

Follow-up

EOP-49 filed for the drifted line citations in ADR-024/ADR-025 and the "first statement of all three" ordinal, including two anchors this slice itself invalidated when the flag key moved from application.yml:91 to :99.

Gate 5 will want six things when the flag-on story reaches it: ADR-026 off Proposed with observability actually implemented; EOP-48 fixed; EOP-15 scoring and completing a hand; the security auditor's seven conditions each discharged and cited; TrickPlayEnabledIntegrationTest grown into the positive mirror of all six beans and five routes; and a fresh documentation sweep, because flipping the flag turns every "ships false" sentence in the corpus stale in a single commit.

EOP-14's five slices are now all merged or in review. EOP-15 (scoring and end of game) is unblocked once #49 lands.

EOP-15.renderedBody:
Delivery plan — three slices off main, all behind eop.features.trick-play

EOP-14 is now Done (all five slices merged, PR #49 landed as 4a99387), so this story is unblocked. Moving to In Progress.

Interpretation decisions taken before any code

These are the reading choices this story rests on. They are written down first so the review gates can challenge the interpretation rather than only the implementation.

  1. Threat point iff `threatLinked`; the trick point goes to the winner regardless of linkage. The ticket says so outright, and it matches shipped behaviour — Trick.winningPlay() ignores threatLinked entirely. The whitepaper's "only count the highest card which was actually connected" is therefore read as a restriction on scoring, not on winning a trick. The beginner-relaxation variant is noted as a possible future toggle, not built, per the ticket.
  1. A linked threat that names no component still scores. TrickPlay's javadoc explicitly hands this open decision to EOP-15, so here is the answer and the reasoning: the shipped rule keys on the threat being linked, not on naming a component; PRD line 146 records that the application holds no model of the system, so it cannot validate a component name; making a score hinge on unvalidated client free text sits badly with "a client must never assert its own score"; and the Score Card's Component(s) column may legitimately be blank.
  1. The running score is derived from resolved tricks; only the final outcome is stored. The score is a pure function of the trick_play rows plus each trick's winner_play_id, so deriving it cannot drift from the play that produced it. What gets persisted at completion is the terminal status and the standings, because SessionStatus.COMPLETED already means "every trick has been played and the score is final". This reads the ticket's "computed and stored server-side" as a statement about authority — the server computes, never the client — rather than a requirement for a running-score table. Flagging it explicitly because it is the one decision here that reinterprets the ticket's wording; it is reversible, since a stored projection would be purely additive.
  1. The facilitator's early end is `COMPLETED`, not `ABANDONED`. The ticket says the highest score wins when play ends, so an early end is a finish. ABANDONED stays reserved for expiry and abandonment (EOP-22).
  1. Ties are shown as ties, never broken. Trick-level ties cannot occur — the deck holds no duplicate suit+rank — but score ties are ordinary, and the ticket requires them displayed as ties.
  1. No `ScoreRepository`. Names come from SessionRepository.findById → GameSession.players(); the tricks come from one new read method on TrickRepository, because reading tricks is that port's job. A port that only re-read tricks would be a port for nothing. Any new method keeps ADR-024's rule: no acting player in any signature — authorising the requester stays the use case's job.
  1. Richer scoring stays out. The abandoned v0.21 system (4 for a threat on your own card, 3/2/1 on others', +2 face, +3 ace) was dropped because players could not compute it at the table, not because it played worse — and a server removes that constraint. Worth recording as an option; explicitly not built here.

Slices

Slice A — the scoring rule, pure domain. New entity types computing points from resolved tricks. Zero framework imports, no routes, no schema, purely additive. Unit tests cover the three awkward cases the ticket names: an unlinked play, a trick won by a trump, and a tie.

Slice B — read the running score. docs/api/openapi.yml first, then the new TrickRepository read method, a GetScoreUseCase, {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

/score}}, and a DTO reconstructible into the Score Card's five columns (Name | Points | Card | Component(s) | Notes on Threat). Membership required — a score is not information a stranger is owed.

Slice C — end of game. Changeset 006-*.xml, SessionRepository.recordCompleted in the existing compare-and-swap style, the automatic COMPLETED transition keyed off nextLeaderSeat already being empty at resolution, the facilitator's early end, winner and ties in the read model, the ADR, and a documentation sweep.

Two things noted now so they are not forgotten at the end

  • This story makes several existing documents false in the present tense — exactly what got three EOP-14 slices rejected repeatedly. The known list: SessionStatus's class javadoc ("nothing here advances a session out of IN_PROGRESS"), the eop.features.trick-play comment block in application.yml which names EOP-15 as an outstanding blocker, and TrickState.handComplete's "says nothing about the score". Every cardinal count of use cases, ports and routes gets re-derived from source rather than read for plausibility.
  • Flipping `eop.features.trick-play` is not this story's job (ADR-028). The flag ships false; flag-on remains its own story, and this story discharges one of its predecessors.

All five DoD gates run on every slice.

EOP-17.renderedBody:
Delivered — merged to main as be2d0ef via PR #53

https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/53

What changed

GlobalExceptionHandler (org.maglez.eop.adapter.web) gained the two missing mappings. Both escape paths — JoinSessionUseCase:160 rethrowing the last SeatAlreadyTakenException after MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS, and CreateSessionUseCase:110 rethrowing JoinCodeUnavailableException after its 5-attempt budget — previously fell through to handleUnexpected(Exception) and answered 500 with a full stack trace at ERROR.

Exception Status Body Logging
SeatAlreadyTakenException 409 "The lobby filled while you were joining" fixed detail, ProblemDetail DEBUG, no throwable
JoinCodeUnavailableException 503 "No lobby could be opened" + Retry-After: 5 fixed detail, ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> WARN, with throwable

Acceptance criteria

  • Scenario 1 — seat contention exhausts retries. 409 with a human-readable body, no stack trace at ERROR. SessionContentionIntegrationTest.shouldAnswerSeatContentionWith409 proves it over HTTP; GlobalExceptionHandlerTest.shouldLogSeatContentionAtDebugWithoutATrace pins Level.DEBUG and getThrowableProxy() null.
  • Scenario 2 — join-code collision exhausts retries. 503 with Retry-After, no stack trace at ERROR. shouldAnswerJoinCodeExhaustionWith503 asserts header().string("Retry-After", "5"); shouldLogJoinCodeExhaustionAtWarnRatherThanError pins Level.WARN.
  • Scenario 3 — existing mappings unaffected. shouldLeaveTheUncontestedPathUntouched drives create-then-join with both stub switches closed (201 then 200); the pre-existing 49-test handler suite is unchanged and green.

Four decisions worth recording

  1. Neither response echoes its exception's message. SeatAlreadyTakenException.getMessage() names the internal session UUID and seat order, and a joining caller supplied only a join code — so it never held either. JoinCodeUnavailableException's message describes our own generator colliding with itself. Both details are compile-time literals.
  2. The log-level asymmetry is derived from provokability, not severity. DEBUG-without-throwable for the 409 because a WARN-plus-stack-trace would merely relocate the log-flooding amplifier this ticket exists to remove; WARN-with-throwable for the 503 because that path is not caller-provokable and each occurrence is genuine evidence the live-lobby count is approaching what a ~30-bit code space bears. Neither logs at ERROR.
  3. The 503 is a capacity statement, not a fault. Five seconds is documented in the constant's own Javadoc as a guess that only has to be defensible — there is no queue draining at a known rate to derive a figure from.
  4. A unit test could not have caught this defect. What escaped was an absent handler, and an absent @ExceptionHandler is invisible to a test that names the handler it expects. Hence SessionContentionIntegrationTest, which drives the full web adapter through a @Primary SessionRepository decorator (hand-written, no Mockito, per house convention) and so proves Spring dispatches to the new methods.

Verification

./mvnw -o verify — BUILD SUCCESS, Tests run: 915, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0; SpotBugs BugInstance size is 0; JaCoCo All coverage checks have been met over 109 classes; checkstyle clean. GlobalExceptionHandler is at 100% instruction (438), line (133) and method (32) coverage. CI on PR #53: build, ui, image all pass.

Definition of Done — five of five gates approved

Gate Verdict Commit reviewed
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE 270dacf
@tester-api APPROVE 4cad0df
@security-auditor APPROVE f06e5ea
@code-reviewer APPROVE f06e5ea

@tester-api initially REJECTED 270dacf over Retry-After being declared without required: true on both ServiceUnavailable and the pre-existing TooManyRequests, while the implementation sets the header unconditionally. That rejection was actioned, not downgraded — 4cad0df fixed both declarations and the gate was re-dispatched and converted to APPROVE.

@architecture-guardian declined to write a new ADR and justified it: ADR-005 enumerates no status codes, so choosing one cannot depart from it — and its Mitigation clause ("unit tests cover every known domain exception → HTTP status mapping") means the missing handlers were a violation this change restores. It instead amended ADR-019, which already records the sibling 429-with-Retry-After inline beside the retry design, and added terminal HTTP exits to both retry loops in docs/architecture/runtime-view.md. No C4 change: the handler is a responsibility box that lists no statuses.

docs/api/openapi.yml gained the new shared ServiceUnavailable response, '503' on POST /api/v1/sessions, and a correction of the Conflict prose from thirteen 409 cases to fourteen — a count three separate reviewers verified independently against the source.

Flag position unchanged

eop.features.session-lifecycle remains OFF. This ticket was a gate on EOP-25, not the flip.

Five follow-up tickets filed for pre-existing findings

Reviewers surfaced nine findings, none introduced by this change:

  • EOP-54 — handleSessionFull echoes the internal session UUID and capacity via exception.getMessage(). A sibling 409 on this very endpoint already leaks exactly what this ticket set out to protect. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-55 — handleSessionNotJoinable echoes the session UUID and lifecycle status. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-56 — POST /api/v1/sessions is entirely unthrottled. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-57 — the logback-spring.xml that observability.md mandates does not exist; production runs at default INFO plain-text, which is what makes the new DEBUG line safe incidentally rather than by design.
  • EOP-58 — docs/NITs, including runtime-view.md:357 claiming the join returns 201 when it returns 200.

One correction to this ticket's own premise. @security-auditor established that SeatAlreadyTakenException is effectively unreachable over HTTP: MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS = 8 exceeds GameSession.MAXIMUM_PLAYERS = 6 and SessionRepository exposes no seat-vacating method, so a joiner loses at most five races before its own re-read yields the already-mapped SessionFullException. The claim that ~20 concurrent joins force the path at will does not hold. The escaped 500 was a real code defect and the mapping is correct defence-in-depth, but the log-flooding amplifier it was credited with removing was largely theoretical — and that unwritten attempts > capacity invariant is captured in EOP-58.

EOP-18.renderedBody:
Severity re-assessment from the EOP-10 review (PR #36) — @security-auditor

This story is more severe than it was filed, because of a defect found during the review and now filed as EOP-26.

As filed, the fail-open on saturation reads as an accidental degradation: if enough distinct addresses appear organically, the tracking map fills and the limiter stops protecting. That framing assumes an attacker has to wait for that condition.

They do not. ClientAddresses.of(HttpServletRequest) honours X-Forwarded-For with no trusted-proxy check anywhere in the codebase, so when the application is reached without Caddy in front — the normal ./mvnw spring-boot:run mode — a caller supplies the value the limiter keys on. That means an attacker can deliberately fill all 10,000 address keys on demand and switch the limiter off wholesale, in seconds, rather than waiting for organic load.

A fail-open an attacker can trigger at will is a different class of defect from one that only manifests under load. Two consequences for planning:

  • EOP-26 should land before this story, or at least alongside it. Making the check-and-record atomic and fail-closed is the right fix, but it protects a bucket the attacker can currently sidestep entirely.
  • The fail-closed behaviour this story adds becomes considerably more valuable once EOP-26 lands, because saturation stops being attacker-controlled.

No change to this story's acceptance criteria is required — the work described is still exactly right. This is a priority and sequencing note.

EOP-24.renderedBody:
*PR opened: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/112* — branch EOP-24-widen-join-code-to-8-chars, three commits.

Scope items, all four delivered

  1. `JoinCode.LENGTH` 6 → 8. This is the only production switch — SecureRandomJoinCodeGenerator, GameSessionJpaEntity's @Column(length = JoinCode.LENGTH) and three test helpers all derive from the constant and widened for free.
  2. `2026-08-22--widen-join-code-to-8-characters.xml` widens join_code to VARCHAR(8) behind a columnExists precondition, valid on H2 and PostgreSQL 17 (modifyDataType emits ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN on both; LENGTH() and || are ANSI). Both changesets carry <rollback>.
  3. Generator Javadoc corrected to the proxy-pool model. The "centuries" claim is gone from InMemoryJoinAttemptLimiter — it says explicitly that the earlier arithmetic assumed the attacker owned one address.
  4. ADR-019 amended with the entropy calculation, the attack model and the rationale for eight.

A correction worth recording on the ticket

The ticket's own framing was right and the ADR's was wrong in a way worth naming: ADR-019's Consequences section had said "Eight characters would have made the limiter a courtesy. Six makes it a control. Anyone tempted to remove or weaken it must lengthen the code first." The amendment quotes that verbatim and explains it did not survive the arithmetic — the per-code window never fires against enumeration at any length, because each guess lands in its own fresh bucket. So the limiter was not downgraded: length bounds how much of the keyspace a blind search must cover, the limiter bounds how fast any one address covers it. ADR-021 is untouched, since header rotation defeats the rate bound at any code length.

Three related ADRs were corrected by amendment rather than rewriting: ADR-021 keeps its verbatim quotation of the old "primary security control" wording and marks it historical; ADR-033's claim that a flood would consume "every six-character join code" is now false at 40 bits (43M rows/day needs ~70 years to exhaust 1.1e12), so its decision is restated on the harm that was always larger — unbounded game_session growth by an unauthenticated caller; ADR-023's aside is now length-neutral so it cannot go stale again.

One design decision the ticket did not anticipate

GameSessionJpaEntity.toDomain() calls the strict JoinCode constructor, so a stored six-character row would throw IllegalArgumentException and 500 the reconnect path {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

}} for already-seated players. The changeset therefore pads legacy rows (join_code || '00') rather than deleting them: padding keeps every foreign key intact, cannot collide with uq_game_session_join_code, and preserves reconnect. Codes already read aloud stop parsing and 404 indistinguishably, bounded by ADR-036's 24-hour TTL.

Two defects found and fixed in passing

  • DeckTrimMigrationRoundTripTest hardcoded rollback(1)/rollback(2), counting backwards from the end of the changelog — which a new dated changelog breaks, since <includeAll> orders changes/ alphabetically. All six call sites now use a dynamic changesetsAppliedFrom(connection, filename, floor) helper, the idiom SessionExpiryMigrationTest and TrickPlaySchemaRoundTripTest already used, parameterised rather than duplicated a third time.
  • MigrationTestFixtures derived its code with a hardcoded substring(0, 6); it now uses JoinCode.LENGTH.

Acceptance criteria

Criterion Status
Codes are 8 characters Met — JoinCode.LENGTH = 8, pinned by a new shouldCarryFortyBitsOfEntropy test computing log2(ALPHABET.length()) * LENGTH
VARCHAR widened in a valid migration Met — H2 and PostgreSQL 17, with rollback
Javadoc corrected Met — 9 production files; "centuries" removed
ADR-019 records the rationale Met — plus ADR-021/023/033 amendments and the ADR index
Existing join-code tests pass Met — JoinCodeTest rewritten, plus 2 new tests
./mvnw verify passes Met — Tests run: 1274, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, BUILD SUCCESS; JaCoCo 96.9% instruction / 88.7% branch against 80/70 gates

npm run verify in ui/ also passes (223 tests). No functional front-end change was required — JoinSessionForm.tsx validates only for non-emptiness and there is no maxLength or pattern anywhere in ui/src.

Definition of Done — all five gates approved

@tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor and @architecture-guardian approved on the first pass. @code-reviewer rejected on the substring(0, 8) literal, three stale rollback-depth comments and a JoinCode Javadoc example that illustrated nothing; all were fixed in 3a362c7 and it re-approved.

One recorded non-finding: @security-auditor recalculated the exposure window as 0.1–0.7 days and suggested the documented 1.5–7.5 days was over-conservative. That recalculation inverted the division. Expected guesses = keyspace ÷ live lobbies = 1.07e8 down to 2.14e7; at 1.44e7 guesses/day that is 7.4 down to 1.5 days. @code-reviewer independently confirmed the range is exact, so every documented figure is unchanged.

Honest limits, carried into the ADR

The ticket's own caveat is preserved rather than dropped: the 10–50 concurrent-lobby assumption is load-bearing, so a near-empty demo is 10–50× slower to attack. The prize is a seat in a card game and there is no authentication anywhere (ADR-015). Padded legacy rows still carry 30 bits, though they were already circulating and expire within 24 hours. Changeset 002's rollback would also truncate a genuinely generated code ending 00, so the two rollbacks are documented to run together (rollbackCount=2) or not at all. The direction is right and the change was cheap, which is why it was made — it was not an incident.

Awaiting human approval on the PR.

From the EOP-10 review (PR #36), where all five reviewers signed off on the code but three new defects were accepted as follow-ups.

This story was gated on EOP-17 through EOP-22. Two additions:

The other review follow-ups — EOP-28 (handleIllegalArgument), EOP-29 (contract polish), EOP-30 (correlation id), EOP-31 (documentation sweep) — are deliberately not gates on this flag. None of them affects whether the session lifecycle is safe to expose.

PR #40 opened from EOP-26-trusted-proxy-forwarded-for. ./mvnw verify green: exit 0, 386 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs 0, Checkstyle 0, JaCoCo met.

All four acceptance scenarios covered. Scenario 1 and 3 by ClientAddressResolverTest and TrustedProxiesTest; Scenario 2 by HeaderHonouredFromTrustedProxy; Scenario 4 by RotationAttackBlocked, which drives ten failing joins with a distinct join code each time so only the per-address counter can produce the refusal. Remediation was the explicit allow-list option from the ticket notes, not server.forward-headers-strategy — though that property is now pinned to none as a fence, because RemoteIpValve's default internalProxies covers 172.16.0.0/12, which contains this project's own Compose subnet.

The strongest evidence that this defect was real came out of the work rather than the analysis: the integration suite's freshAddress() helper had been getting its per-test throttle isolation from the vulnerability itself — a test choosing its own rate-limiter key from outside the process, which is precisely the attack. Closing the hole broke sixteen previously-passing tests. A green build had been evidence the bug was still present.

Review gates: 4 of 5 approved. @security-auditor (who raised this on PR #36), @code-reviewer, @tester-unit-and-quality and @architecture-guardian all approved with evidence. The auditor built an InetAddressResolverProvider spy proving zero DNS lookups leak, with a negative control confirming the guard is load-bearing, and verified from bytecode that RemoteIpValve is not installed.

⚠️ @tester-api did not produce a usable sign-off across four dispatches — no file:line findings, no build exit code, no order-independence runs. I am not recording that gate as passed. Filed separately as an agent-configuration issue; the substantive API-boundary questions were answered with evidence by @security-auditor, so this is not believed to be a code risk. PR should not merge until that is resolved.

Two findings worth noting for the record, both caught by @architecture-guardian rejecting twice — correctly:

  1. IpLiteralsTest hard-coded %lo0, green on macOS and red on `ubuntu-latest` where the loopback is lo. It would have broken the build on merge while passing every local review.
  2. My own replacement fix was also wrong: selecting the first network interface passed only because a VPN utun4 sorted first. The platform needs a scope id, which exists only on an interface carrying an IPv6 link-local address.

ADR-021 records the decision plus eight known limitations. An earlier revision of it claimed DNS-free parsing "by construction"; that claim was measured false (a cold colon-bearing hostname lookup blocked a request thread for 5020 ms) and is now explicitly retracted rather than quietly deleted.

EOP-27.renderedBody:
Premise correction before this lands — the console was never actually served, and AC2 cannot be met without adding the attack surface this ticket exists to remove.

What I found. I wrote the acceptance tests first, including the AC2 "console is reachable" test, and it failed: with the opt-in set, /h2-console was still 404 and no console servlet bean existed. Investigation was conclusive:

  • The full test classpath contains h2-2.4.240.jar and 33 spring-boot 4.1.0 modules, and `spring-boot-h2console` is not among them.
  • No class named H2Console exists on any jar on the classpath, and no AutoConfiguration.imports file on the classpath mentions the console.
  • Maven Central confirms org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console exists for 4.0.0–4.1.0. Spring Boot 4 modularised the console's autoconfiguration out of spring-boot-autoconfigure into that separate module. Inspecting the jar: it registers ServletRegistrationBean<JakartaWebServlet> h2Console() from org.springframework.boot.h2console.autoconfigure.H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration.

So spring.h2.console.enabled: true was inert — no class on the classpath ever read it. There was no live unauthenticated-SQL endpoint at any point. This is the same failure mode as the Liquibase defect already recorded in the changelog: Boot 4 modularisation leaving configuration that reads as active but is never consulted.

Why the ticket is still worth doing, and what I changed instead. The defect is not a live endpoint but security-sensitive configuration that says yes. One transitive dependency, or one developer adding the module for local convenience, and the exposure arrives silently with consent already granted and nothing prompting a review. So:

  • application.yml now pins enabled: false with the reasoning attached — the exposure it would be, that the module is absent today, and why the line stays rather than being deleted: whoever adds the module has to change a line that says why it is off, instead of inheriting a default. The dead path: /h2-console is removed.
  • application-prod.yml keeps its own redundant false as a second independent guard, now commented as deliberate.
  • src/test/resources/application.properties no longer pins spring.h2.console.enabled=false. That override would have made any "console is absent" assertion pass because of the test's own configuration rather than the shipped default — defeating AC3. The suite now reads what ships.
  • H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest (real port, JDK HttpClient, since MockMvc returns 404 for a servlet registration whether or not it is registered) asserts 404 on both /h2-console and /h2-console/, that the h2Console bean is absent, that the resolved property is false, and — the load-bearing one — that H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration is not on the classpath. That last assertion is the tripwire: it is the only one that can fail today, and it fires the day somebody adds the module, so the decision happens at review time rather than in an incident.

AC2 is not satisfiable as written and I have not faked it. "Given a developer sets the explicit opt-in property, the console is reachable" requires adding spring-boot-h2console to pom.xml. Adding an unauthenticated-SQL servlet in order to demonstrate that we have turned it off would be an own-goal, and it is a dependency decision that deserves its own ticket rather than arriving as a side effect of a hardening story. I propose AC2 be re-read as: enabling the console is a deliberate act that requires adding a dependency, and the build refuses until somebody revisits the guard. That is stronger than a property opt-in — it cannot be done by accident.

Honest limitation, flagged for the reviewers. While the module is absent, the 404, absent-bean and property assertions cannot fail — they are vacuous by construction. They are kept because the tripwire converts them: the day it fires and the module is added deliberately, they become the assertions that the guard actually holds, and they are already in place. The test's Javadoc says this in those terms rather than claiming three independent guards.

Also fixed, because they promised something that does not exist: docs/devops/local-development.md advertised a console at http://localhost:8080/h2-console with sa and no password; ADR-008 recorded "H2 console available at /h2-console in dev profile" — and there has never been a dev profile either (ADR-012 fixes the set at {{

{default, prod}

}}). Both are corrected, ADR-008 by in-place amendment per the ADR README convention, with the index row updated.

Out of scope, deliberately left for EOP-31: local-development.md and ADR-008 name DATASOURCE_URL/DATASOURCE_USER/DATASOURCE_PASSWORD for the default profile while application.yml and .env.example use DB_URL/DB_USERNAME/DB_PASSWORD. The console opt-in was also deliberately not added to .env.example, which is copied to /opt/eop/.env on the deployment target — a security-sensitive toggle does not belong in a file that ships to the host.

EOP-27.renderedBody:
Review complete — PR #37 approved by all five reviewers, follow-ups filed

PR: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/37 (2 commits: 904259a, 6a4fb71). ./mvnw verify green — 304 tests, checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo 80%.

All five mandatory sign-offs obtained: @tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor, @code-reviewer, @architecture-guardian.

The security auditor recanted its own finding

The CRITICAL raised during the EOP-10 / PR #36 review was factually wrong, and the auditor said so plainly after re-verifying the premise correction three independent ways: it scanned all 129 jars on the test classpath for H2Console (0 hits), grepped every jar's AutoConfiguration.imports for h2 (0 lines), and decompiled spring-boot-h2console-4.1.0.jar from Maven Central to confirm the FQCN, the h2Console bean name and the spring.h2.console.enabled property key all match what the tripwire asserts.

Two findings that strengthen the ticket rather than weaken it:

  • `h2-2.4.240.jar` already ships all 13 `org.h2.server.web` classes, including JakartaWebServlet, inside the production artifact. So the autoconfiguration's @ConditionalOnClass gate is already satisfied — only the autoconfig module was missing. The "one dependency away" framing in the fix comment is understated, not overstated.
  • A negative control I had not run. The auditor mutated application.yml line 38 back to enabled: true and re-ran: Tests run: 4, Failures: 1, shouldResolveTheShippedDefaultToFalse FAILED, BUILD FAILURE. So deleting the `spring.h2.console.enabled=false` override from `src/test/resources/application.properties` was the single most valuable line in this PR — without it the mutation would have passed silently. My original Javadoc undersold this by claiming only the tripwire could fail; commit 6a4fb71 corrects that account.

AC2 — accepted as deliberately unsatisfied

The security auditor endorsed the re-reading rather than requiring the dependency: adding spring-boot-h2console to make a checkbox green would put the exact artifact this ticket exists to keep off the classpath onto it, in the production dependency graph, guarded only by a property — trading a documented latent risk for a live one. Enabling the console now requires a dependency change plus editing a guard that explains why it is off, which is a stronger consent mechanism than a property toggle.

It also declined to require a maven-enforcer ban in this PR, reasoning that a prohibition with no sanctioned escape hatch trains people to run -Denforcer.skip=true or hand-roll Server.createWebServer(). Deferred to EOP-34 as an addition alongside the tripwire, never a swap.

Follow-up tickets filed

  • EOP-32 — Correct the dev/test profile fiction at its source in .opencode/rules/ and re-sync the ADR index. This is where ADR-008's false consequence almost certainly originated: .opencode/rules/configuration.md:5 names three profiles, two of which have never existed, and that file is injected into every agent's context every session. Also covers .opencode/rules/caching.md:7, SETUP.md:138 (the same fiction sitting inside the accepted-risks register), the feature-flag naming drift, and two stale ADR index rows.
  • EOP-33 — Record the Spring Boot 4 autoconfiguration modularisation trap where it will actually be read. Second occurrence after spring-boot-liquibase; all four existing mentions are incident write-ups nobody consults before adding a property.
  • EOP-34 — Harden the H2 dependency surface: h2 to test scope once prod is Postgres-only, optionally ban the console autoconfiguration module. Closes the hand-registration path that no control in EOP-27 covers.

Ready for human approval and merge.

EOP-28.renderedBody:
*PR open and awaiting human approval: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/111*

Branch EOP-28-narrow-illegal-argument-handler, two commits (fbef32c, 0128493).

What changed

A new org.maglez.eop.entity.InvalidInputException now marks the rejections that are genuinely a caller's to fix, and GlobalExceptionHandler maps only that type — keeping 400 and the "Invalid request" title, and adding a LOG.warn so even a legitimate rejection leaves a trace. The old @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class) is gone, so a library-thrown IAE (including NumberFormatException) now falls through to handleUnexpected for a generic 500 and the LOG.error it was previously denied.

It extends `IllegalArgumentException` rather than `RuntimeException`, inverting the house pattern of all 35 existing domain exceptions deliberately. The persistence adapters are @Repository beans, so Spring's translation rewrites an IAE raised while reconstituting an entity from a row into a DataAccessException — the logged 500 a corrupt row deserves. A value object cannot tell whether it is being built from a request or a row, so leaning on that already-tested mechanism is what stops a DB-derived message being echoed as a 400. Extending RuntimeException would have escaped translation and merely relocated this defect.

Scope, from a reachability audit of all 60 throw sites

Only three types had a caller-reachable guard: PageQuery (all 3 converted), DisplayName (all 3), TrickPlay (6 text guards; seatOrder left alone as an internal invariant on a credential-resolved value). Everything else stays on the bare JDK type and so correctly becomes a logged 500 rather than today's silent 400.

Worth recording: the reconstitution guards were never producing 400s — @Repository translation already caught them, pinned by three existing integration tests. The real holes were the use-case and web-layer paths.

Acceptance criteria

  • Scenario 1 — our guards → 400 with the guard's own message, now with a WARN. ✅
  • Scenario 2 — a library-thrown IAE matches no handler, falls to handleUnexpected, gets the generic text. ✅
  • Scenario 3 — rejections at WARN, faults at ERROR; nothing reaches a caller unlogged. ✅

Tests

IllegalArgumentDispatchIntegrationTest drives real Spring dispatch and asserts the contrast — a bare IAE → 500 with no message echo, an InvalidInputException → 400 with it. Only the contrast is evidence; either assertion alone would pass on the broken code. A reflection guard, shouldMapNoForeignExceptionTypeApartFromTheCatchAll, encodes the invariant whose absence was the actual defect, failing if any handler maps a type this project does not own. And 19 assertions were repointed to assertThatExceptionOfType(InvalidInputException.class) so a silent revert of a guard conversion can no longer pass.

./mvnw clean verify → BUILD SUCCESS, 1272 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo all checks met.

Documentation

ADR-048 records the decision and states the cost plainly: the layer a throw passes through now decides the outcome. CHANGELOG.md updated under [Unreleased] → Fixed.

Definition of Done — 5 of 5 approved

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE — after one REJECT, remediated in 0128493
@tester-api APPROVE
@security-auditor APPROVE — 4 LOW findings; both halves of the original EOP-10 finding confirmed closed
@code-reviewer APPROVE — 2 warnings, both since remediated
@architecture-guardian APPROVE — authored ADR-048

The rejection is worth recording rather than glossing: @tester-unit-and-quality found that the first attempt's scenario-2 and scenario-3 tests were tautological — they called handleUnexpected directly, which has always returned a generic 500, so they passed on the old code too. It also found that because the new type IS-A IllegalArgumentException, every existing assertThatIllegalArgumentException() passed whether a guard threw the new type or the bare one. @code-reviewer raised that second point independently. Both are now closed.

Known limits

  • Nothing detects the opposite mistake — a new caller-input guard written with a bare IllegalArgumentException. Enforced by review.
  • TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter.seatToWrite stays on the JDK type for an unrelated reason: converting it to an org.maglez.eop.entity type would add an eleventh origin to the set TrickPlayExceptionOriginTest derives, and its numberWord helper stops at ten.

EOP-31.renderedBody:
Item 1 is resolved by EOP-120 — the inaccurate IdentityTokenHash Javadoc is gone, and the claim it made is now true rather than merely retracted.

The comment asserted that "comparison happens as an indexed database lookup rather than in Java, so there is no meaningful timing side channel in this type". That named a mechanism the code does not contain. The real path is ResolvePlayerUseCase → GameSession.playerByTokenHash → Player.isIdentifiedBy → the record's generated equals → String.equals on hex text: a short-circuiting byte-wise comparison, in memory, over at most six players. uq_player_identity_token_hash enforces uniqueness and is never a lookup path — PlayerJpaRepository declares exactly one query method, by session id.

Rather than delete the claim, EOP-120 made it true: IdentityTokenHash now overrides equals to compare through MessageDigest.isEqual over the US-ASCII bytes of the hex value, with a matching hashCode. Verified against this JDK's own MessageDigest source that there is no early return on a length mismatch, and that the one short-circuit (lenB == 0) is unreachable given the 64-character constructor check.

Nothing exploitable was closed, and the record says so. An attacker supplies a plaintext token, not a digest, so steering the compared bytes needs SHA-256 preimage work; the token is 256 bits of SecureRandom. The defect was documentary — a future lower-entropy credential (a rejoin PIN, a short reconnect code) added to this seam would have inherited a written guarantee that was never true.

The same false claim turned out to exist at three further sites, each found by a review gate rather than by the original sweep, and all three are now corrected: PlayerJpaEntity's column Javadoc, an XML comment sitting directly above the addUniqueConstraint in 003-session-lifecycle.xml, and a residual @return the digest to store and to look up by in IdentityTokenHash itself. Liquibase Golden Rule 1 did not block the migration edit — ChangeSet.generateCheckSum() digests only changes and SQL visitors, never comments, confirmed by bytecode.

Also recorded durably, because a prohibition in a Javadoc comment is not enough (per ADR-020 and ADR-027): ADR-015 now carries an amendment stating that comparison is constant-time in memory, that no lookup path resolves a digest, and that no hash-based collection may be keyed on IdentityTokenHash or Player — a HashMap compares the cached int before calling equals, which would quietly bypass the constant-time comparison.

The other six items on this ticket are untouched and remain open.

Closing EOP-31. All seven findings are disposed of: three fixed, four explicitly closed with a recorded reason. None silently dropped, which was this ticket's acceptance criterion.

Delivered on branch EOP-31-hygiene-sweep, commit 5330a19, parent d4deccf. Pull request 106. Five files, 43 insertions, 6 deletions: .env.example, SETUP.md, src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/GameSession.java, docs/adr/README.md, CHANGELOG.md.

THE THREE FIXES

Item 2, sample passwords. Four keys now ship the literal placeholder CHANGE_ME — the Grafana admin password, the InfluxDB password, and the Postgres and datasource passwords. DB_PASSWORD is deliberately left empty and SETUP.md now says why: it pairs with the sa username against in-memory H2, and the DB_ variable set is consumed only by the default profile, which hard-pins the H2 driver. The container path uses a disjoint variable set and never receives DB_-prefixed values at all. SETUP.md also gained the instruction the template hazard actually needed, because it previously told the developer to copy the file and never to replace anything: grep the copied file for CHANGE_ME and replace every hit before starting the stack.

Item 3, the redundant capacity re-check in GameSession.join(). Kept, not removed, and documented as deliberate. The ground is the defence-in-depth rule in the repository's own security rules: an entity must hold its own invariant regardless of the sequence it happens to be called in, and a future caller that seats a player without first asking for a seat number would otherwise seat a seventh. The false half was in nextSeatOrder()'s Javadoc, whose closing sentence claimed "Keeping the capacity rule here means one place states it" — falsified by the duplicate thirty lines below it since both were written. That sentence is gone and its replacement forecloses the regression by name. No executable line changed; @security-auditor proved that by diffing comment-stripped source (identical, 165 lines each) and hashing the extracted guard lines (same SHA on both commits).

Item 6, the ADR-014 through-Caddy claim. The index row now dates the observation to 2026-08-05 under EOP-10, commit 87d8c49, and scopes it to the two events that existed then. It names what does and does not reproduce it: the stream integration test hits the application directly, ADR-035 records that no test goes through Caddy, and ADR-017's k6 smoke test does go through Caddy but not on the SSE path — verified by grepping the k6 directory for SSE, stream and event references, which returns nothing.

THE FOUR CLOSURES

Item 1 was already closed by EOP-120 and is recorded in an earlier comment here. @architecture-guardian re-verified it rather than taking it on trust: the comparison really is MessageDigest.isEqual, the corrected prose now says "that closes no known exploit" with a scoped reason, and it additionally discloses that hashCode is not constant time.

Item 4 is closed with the residual risk recorded and a follow-up filed as EOP-136. The honest fix is a real engine in the test path and there is no Testcontainers dependency anywhere — a repo-wide grep returns two hits, one of them this story's own changelog entry. The suite runs plain H2 with no PostgreSQL compatibility mode set, against PostgreSQL 17 in production, and eight test sites already mark PostgreSQL behaviour as unmeasured. Adopting a container in the test path collides with the accepted decision not to install Docker Desktop, so it needs its own ADR. EOP-136 has since been widened, on @architecture-guardian's MAJOR finding, to carry the durable record as well as the adoption.

Item 5 is closed as already resolved. The graph was re-indexed and the limitation and re-index trigger are recorded at ADR-011 line 45. One correction to my own closure, which @architecture-guardian was right to make: the graph directory is gitignored, so those node and edge counts are one machine's working directory rather than repository evidence, and the artefact's built-from commit is behind HEAD, which by line 45's own wording is the signal worth acting on rather than the documented steady state. The durable half of this disposition is the trigger at line 45; the re-index is not something a commit can carry.

Item 7 is closed as fixed by events. No "not yet scaffolded" string survives anywhere, and the root AGENTS.md now carries an accurate section describing the front end as shipped.

THREE SELF-CORRECTIONS, ALL THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THIS TICKET EXISTS TO REMOVE

First, this ticket said three sample passwords read as plausible. Measurement says two. @security-auditor independently confirmed it across all seventeen commits of the file's history: two keys held an identical opaque eighteen-character value with every character class and no placeholder marker, while the other two already held the readable phrase choose-a-strong-value. All four were normalised anyway so the must-supply set is enumerable by one token, and widening beyond the two offenders is disclosed rather than slipped in.

Second, item 6 understated its own finding. The claim had not merely gone undated — it had silently widened. Commit 43f0cbc, 2026-08-14, inserted three more events into the same sentence ahead of an unchanged Caddy clause, so a two-event observation came to read as covering five. Verified by pickaxe, which returns exactly two commits for that phrase.

Third, and worst, my own fix shipped a fresh over-attribution. The join() Javadoc claimed the check "is what makes the maximum true of every instance". It is not — the private constructor does that, and all five methods that return a session construct through it. Deleting the check still refuses a seventh player; what it preserves is the 409 the caller is owed instead of the constructor's coarser 400. @security-auditor caught it and rated it MEDIUM precisely because shipping that defect class inside the fix for that defect class is worse than shipping it anywhere else. Corrected, and a grep found the same over-attribution had been copied into the changelog entry, which was corrected too. @security-auditor then swept the tracked tree, the rules directory, the docs, the UI, the test tree and the commit message and confirmed no instance survives.

DEFINITION OF DONE

All five mandatory gates returned VERDICT: APPROVE. @tester-unit-and-quality and @tester-api on 4ab6b80; @code-reviewer and @architecture-guardian on 5330a19; @security-auditor on both, the second pass confirming its own MEDIUM closed. No blocker or major-against-this-commit finding from any gate.

Every gate ran its own cold ./mvnw clean verify rather than accepting mine, and all reproduced the same figures: 1256 tests with zero failures, zero SpotBugs instances, all coverage checks met, zero Checkstyle violations, build success, exit zero. Each also confirmed zero occurrences of "Skipping javadoc generation" and the presence of "No previous run data found" — which matters specifically because this change is comment-only in a Java file, and a warm build can skip the Javadoc gate entirely and prove nothing.

FOLLOW-UPS FILED, NONE BLOCKING

EOP-136 widened to carry the H2-versus-PostgreSQL record as well as the Testcontainers adoption. EOP-137 for the Grafana all-interfaces port binding and its unpinned image tag, both pre-existing in a file this story does not touch. EOP-138 for two measurably falsified figures in ADR-011 and its missing Amendments section. EOP-139 to qualify ADR-014's no-buffering claim, which infers a measurement from the absence of a directive, and to move the widening history out of the index row.
